title: 01. Fundamentals: String Methods — Trim & Padding
summary: Trim methods remove characters from the edges of a string. Padding methods add characters to reach a desired width.
objectives: Critical: strip() removes ANY combination of the given characters!
NOT a prefix/suffix removal — it removes individual chars!

sections.title: CONCEPT EXPLANATION
sections.body:
Trim methods **remove characters** from the edges of a string. Padding methods **add characters** to reach a desired width. These are essential for data cleaning and formatting.

### Trim Methods:

| Method | What It Removes | From Where |
|---|---|---|
| `.strip(chars)` | Whitespace (default) OR specified chars | Both ends |
| `.lstrip(chars)` | Whitespace OR specified chars | Left (beginning) |
| `.rstrip(chars)` | Whitespace OR specified chars | Right (end) |
| `.removeprefix(prefix)` | Exact prefix string (Python 3.9+) | Left only |
| `.removesuffix(suffix)` | Exact suffix string (Python 3.9+) | Right only |

### Padding Methods:

| Method | What It Does |
|---|---|
| `.ljust(width, fillchar)` | Left-justify (pad RIGHT with fillchar) |
| `.rjust(width, fillchar)` | Right-justify (pad LEFT with fillchar) |
| `.center(width, fillchar)` | Center (pad BOTH sides) |
| `.zfill(width)` | Zero-fill (pad LEFT with '0') |

### ⚠️ Critical: `strip()` removes ANY combination of the given characters!
```python
# strip() removes ALL combinations of specified chars from BOTH ends
"   hello   ".strip()           # "hello" — removes spaces
"xxhelloxx".strip("x")         # "hello" — removes all x's from edges
"xxxhelloyyy".strip("xy")      # "hello" — removes x OR y from edges
"...hello...".strip(".")       # "hello"

```

# ⚠️ NOT a prefix/suffix removal — it removes individual chars!
"abcHELLOcba".strip("abc")     # "HELLO" — strips a, b, c chars (any order!)
```

---

```

sections.title: 5 EXAMPLES
sections.body:
### Example 1: `strip()`, `lstrip()`, `rstrip()` — Trimming
```python
# Default: strip whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines)
messy = "   \t Hello World \n   "
print(f"strip():  '{messy.strip()}'")    # 'Hello World'
print(f"lstrip(): '{messy.lstrip()}'")   # 'Hello World \n   '
print(f"rstrip(): '{messy.rstrip()}'")   # '   \t Hello World'

# Strip specific characters
path = "///usr/local/bin///"
print(path.strip("/"))          # "usr/local/bin"
print(path.lstrip("/"))         # "usr/local/bin///"
print(path.rstrip("/"))         # "///usr/local/bin"

# Strip multiple characters (any combination from ends)
data = "...###Hello World###..."
print(data.strip(".#"))         # "Hello World"  ← strips . AND # from both ends

# Practical: Clean CSV data
csv_line = '  "Alice Smith" , "28" , " Hyderabad " '
fields = [f.strip().strip('"') for f in csv_line.split(",")]
print(f"CSV fields: {fields}")   # ['Alice Smith', '28', 'Hyderabad']

# Practical: Clean file content lines
file_content = """
  Line 1 with leading space
  Line 2 with trailing space   
  Line 3 
"""
clean_lines = [line.strip() for line in file_content.split('\n')
               if line.strip()]   # Also filter empty lines
print("Clean lines:", clean_lines)
```

### Example 2: `removeprefix()` and `removesuffix()` (Python 3.9+)
```python
# removeprefix — removes exact prefix (not individual chars like strip!)
url = "https://www.example.com"
print(url.removeprefix("https://"))    # "www.example.com"
print(url.removeprefix("http://"))     # "https://www.example.com" — no change!

# removesuffix — removes exact suffix
filename = "report_2026.pdf"
print(filename.removesuffix(".pdf"))   # "report_2026"
print(filename.removesuffix(".csv"))   # "report_2026.pdf" — no change!

# Why removeprefix/removesuffix are better than strip() for this:
# strip() removes INDIVIDUAL CHARS, not the whole prefix!
url2 = "https://example.com"
print(url2.strip("https://"))   # WRONG! "example.com" — but also strips s, h, t, p!
# If url started with "sheet" it would also strip 's', 'h', 'e', 't'!

print(url2.removeprefix("https://"))  # CORRECT! Only removes the exact string

# Practical: processing file lists
filenames = [
    "test_login.py",
    "test_payment.py",
    "test_profile.py",
    "utils.py",
    "models.py"
]

# Extract test names (remove "test_" prefix and ".py" suffix)
test_names = [f.removeprefix("test_").removesuffix(".py")
              for f in filenames if f.startswith("test_")]
print(f"Test names: {test_names}")   # ['login', 'payment', 'profile']
```

### Example 3: `ljust()`, `rjust()`, `center()`, `zfill()` — Padding
```python
# ljust — left justify (pad RIGHT) — text flows left, spaces on right
print("Alice".ljust(15))           # "Alice          "
print("Alice".ljust(15, "-"))      # "Alice----------"

# rjust — right justify (pad LEFT) — text flows right, spaces on left
print("Alice".rjust(15))           # "          Alice"
print("42".rjust(8, "0"))          # "00000042"

# center — center text
print("REPORT".center(30))         # "            REPORT            "
print("REPORT".center(30, "="))    # "============REPORT============"

# zfill — zero-fill (always pads with '0' on left)
print("42".zfill(8))               # "00000042"
print("-42".zfill(8))              # "-0000042" — handles sign!
print("3.14".zfill(8))             # "00003.14"

# Generate formatted table
print("\n=== Employee Table ===")
headers = ["Name", "Department", "Salary"]
rows    = [
    ["Alice Smith",     "Engineering", "₹85,000"],
    ["Veerababu Kumar", "Engineering", "₹91,000"],
    ["Bob Jones",       "Marketing",   "₹72,000"],
]

# Print header
print(f"{'Name':<20} {'Department':<15} {'Salary':>10}")
print("-" * 47)
for name, dept, salary in rows:
    print(f"{name:<20} {dept:<15} {salary:>10}")
```

### Example 4: Real-World Cleaning — Processing Data Files
```python
def clean_tsv_data(raw_data):
    """
    Clean TSV (Tab-Separated Values) data from a messy source.
    Uses strip() extensively.
    """
    clean_records = []

    for line in raw_data.strip().split('\n'):
        if not line.strip():       # Skip empty lines
            continue
        if line.strip().startswith('#'):  # Skip comments
            continue

        fields = line.split('\t')
        if len(fields) < 4:
            continue

        record = {
            "id":      fields[0].strip(),
            "name":    fields[1].strip().title(),
            "email":   fields[2].strip().lower().strip('"'),
            "salary":  fields[3].strip().lstrip('₹').replace(',', ''),
        }

        # Validate after cleaning
        if not record["id"].isdecimal():
            continue
        if "@" not in record["email"]:
            continue

        try:
            record["salary"] = int(record["salary"])
        except ValueError:
            record["salary"] = 0

        clean_records.append(record)

    return clean_records

raw_data = """
# Employee data export
# Generated: 2026-05-02

001\t  ALICE SMITH  \t"Alice@Example.COM"\t₹85,000
002\t veerababu kumar\t  veera@example.com \t91000
003\t  BOB JONES\t"bob@gmail.com   "\t₹72,000  
004\tinvalid-id\tsomeone@ex.com\t50000
"""

records = clean_tsv_data(raw_data)
print("Cleaned Records:")
for r in records:
    print(f"  [{r['id']}] {r['name']:<20} {r['email']:<30} ₹{r['salary']:,}")
```

### Example 5: Formatting with Padding — Reports and Tables
```python
def generate_ascii_report(title, data, columns):
    """
    Generate a nicely formatted ASCII table.
    columns: [(name, width, align)] where align is 'l', 'r', 'c'
    """
    total_width = sum(w for _, w, _ in columns) + len(columns) * 3 + 1
    line = "=" * total_width

    def format_cell(value, width, align):
        value = str(value)[:width]  # Truncate if too long
        if align == 'l':   return value.ljust(width)
        elif align == 'r': return value.rjust(width)
        else:              return value.center(width)

    rows_text = []

    # Header
    header_cells = [format_cell(name, w, a) for name, w, a in columns]
    rows_text.append("| " + " | ".join(header_cells) + " |")
    rows_text.append("|" + "-" * (total_width - 2) + "|")

    # Data rows
    for row in data:
        cells = [format_cell(val, w, a)
                 for (_, w, a), val in zip(columns, row)]
        rows_text.append("| " + " | ".join(cells) + " |")

    # Summary
    report = f"""
{title.center(total_width)}
{line}
{chr(10).join(rows_text)}
{line}
Total records: {len(data)}
"""
    return report

columns = [
    ("Emp ID",     8,  'c'),
    ("Name",       20, 'l'),
    ("Department", 15, 'l'),
    ("Salary",     10, 'r'),
    ("Rating",      7, 'c'),
]
data = [
    ["E001", "Alice Smith",     "Engineering", "₹85,000", "4.5/5"],
    ["E002", "Veerababu Kumar", "Engineering", "₹91,000", "4.8/5"],
    ["E003", "Bob Jones",       "Marketing",   "₹72,000", "4.2/5"],
    ["E004", "Carol White",     "HR",          "₹65,000", "4.0/5"],
]

print(generate_ascii_report("EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE REPORT", data, columns))
```

quiz.explanation: They look similar but work completely differently: strip('abc') treats the argument as a set of characters and removes any combination of those characters from both ends — it removes individual characters 'a', 'b', 'c' in any order, any number of times. removeprefix('abc') treats the argument as an exact string and only removes it if the string starts with exactly that sequence.
